chunks.text: This is a cover page slide/title page from a PDF report or whitepaper, not a data visualization. The title displayed in large bold white text reads **"Navigating the Canadian job market"** with a subtitle in lighter white text reading **"The power of tech & AI skills today and beyond."** There are no numbers, percentages, data points, axis labels, or column headers present on this page, as it is purely a cover design. The visual features a deep purple/violet gradient background with decorative teal/blue dot patterns scattered across the upper right portion. In the lower half, there is a circular-cropped overhead photograph of a person wearing a white long-sleeve striped sweater typing on a black laptop displaying code on its screen, seated at a round wooden table alongside a white coffee mug and a Le Wagon-branded notebook with red pencils. Two logos are visible in the upper left corner: **"le wagon"** (displayed with a red icon featuring a bus/wagon symbol) and **"rhum.hr"** (displayed in a bordered box). The source organizations are therefore **Le Wagon** and **rhum.hr**, which are the co-publishers of this report. The key takeaway from this cover page is that the document focuses on the relevance and importance of technology and artificial intelligence skills within the Canadian employment landscape, targeting job seekers or professionals looking to understand or leverage tech competencies in the current and future job market.

This image is a text-based document page (not a chart, graph, or visual infographic), specifically page 2 of a white paper PDF. The page contains two main sections with headings: **"Context"** and **"Our Process."** The exact numbers and data points visible on this page are: **88%** of companies report difficulty filling essential positions due to a shortage of qualified talent, cited from *Robert Half*; the recruitment data for technology positions is cited from *CompTIA*; and the research period for rhum.hr recruitment mandates is specified as **2024–2025**. There are no axis labels, column headers, bar charts, tables, or scatter plots on this page — it is entirely prose-based. The key insight communicated is that despite economic slowdowns across several sectors, the Canadian job market continues to show strong and growing demand for technical skills — particularly in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and data management — and that 88% of companies struggle to fill essential roles due to a talent shortage, meaning technically skilled professionals remain in high demand. The document was created by **Le Wagon** and **rhum.hr**, and sources cited within the text include **CompTIA** (for technology sector recruitment growth) and **Robert Half** (for the 88% statistic). The footer reads "Le Wagon © – All Rights Reserved" and the page is numbered **2**.

This visual is an infographic/summary slide from a report. The heading is **"Key takeaways"** displayed in bold white text on a dark purple background. There are no charts, graphs, axes, or numerical data points present in this visual — it contains exclusively text-based bullet points and a quote. The seven bullet points read exactly as follows: (1) Hiring is growing across Canada in tech and tech adjacent roles; (2) Technical skills are increasingly in-demand even in traditionally non-technical roles; (3) A blend of technical and non tech skills makes candidates more appealing to employers; (4) The most in-demand tech skills: programming, data management and AI (Machine Learning, NLP, Prompt Engineering...); (5) The most in-demand non tech skills: Interpersonal skills, adaptability, critical thinking and resilience; (6) Artificial intelligence is revolutionizing the job market and forcing both companies and candidates to adapt; (7) Continuing education and acquiring new skills are essential for keeping up with demands. Below the key takeaways box is a pull quote attributed to **Christopher Moreno, CFO of MarineLabs**, which states: *"I think it's important for everyone to understand that technology is rooted in creativity, and that we need creative people, both in how they think and how they solve problems. I've yet to see any evidence suggesting that humans won't be doing these kinds of jobs for at least the next **25 years**."* The only specific number present is **25 years**. The source listed at the bottom is **Le Wagon © – All Rights Reserved**, co-branded with **le wagon** and **rhum hr**, and this is page **3** of the document.

This is an infographic/report page from a PDF document. The title or heading is **"Today's job market roller coaster."** The page contains the following exact numbers and data points: AI jobs grew **15x** between 2012 and 2024; job postings in artificial intelligence increased from **4,000 in 2012 to 57,000 in 2024**, representing a 15-fold increase over twelve years; growth in jobs in software engineering over the next 10 years is **163%**; growth in tech jobs over the next 10 years is **1.8x**; employment in technology occupations in Canada is expected to grow **1.77 times faster** than the national average over the next decade; growth for software engineers is **+163%**; growth for information systems managers is **+153%**; growth for cybersecurity specialists is **+131%**; the proportion of job postings requiring artificial intelligence skills reached **1.8%** in 2024, described as the highest level in the entire dataset analyzed; in 2024, the technology sector employed approximately **1.45 million people**, representing **6.8%** of the Canadian workforce. There are no axis labels or column headers as this is not a chart. The key insight is that despite widespread layoffs following the COVID-19 pandemic boom, Canada's technology sector remains dynamic and growing, with AI-related roles and software engineering experiencing particularly explosive demand. The sources cited are **PwC** (for AI job posting data based on nearly one billion job postings from six continents) and **CompTIA** (for Canadian technology employment projections). The document is published by **Le Wagon** in partnership with **rhum.hr**, and the page is labeled as page **4**.

This visual is an infographic page from a PDF report combining a choropleth map of Canada with a legend showing job vacancy growth rates by province, accompanied by explanatory text sections. The heading reads "Job vacancies in Canada," with a subheading stating "Studies show that despite an economic slowdown in several sectors, job vacancies in the private sector continue to grow across Canada's main provinces." The map section is titled "Job vacancy growth" and displays the following exact data points from the legend: British Columbia 2.9%, Alberta 3%, Saskatchewan 2.9%, Manitoba 2.8%, Ontario 2.4%, Quebec 3.2%, Nova Scotia 3.2%, New Brunswick 3%, Prince Edward Island 3.9%, and Newfoundland and Labrador 2.3%. There are no axis labels as this is a map-based visual rather than a chart. The provinces are shaded in varying tones of purple, with darker shades indicating higher growth rates. The source cited is CFIB (Canadian Federation of Independent Business). The key insight is that Prince Edward Island has the highest job vacancy growth at 3.9%, while Newfoundland and Labrador has the lowest at 2.3%, and Ontario also ranks low at 2.4%. The page also includes a secondary section titled "Tech vs. other sectors," discussing how technical skills in cloud, data, AI, cybersecurity, and automation are now essential across all industries including retail, healthcare, finance, and manufacturing, citing sources Polytechnics Canada and Randstad. The page is numbered 5 and credited to Le Wagon and rhumhr.

This visual is a **table** presented on page 6 of a document published by Le Wagon in partnership with rhum:hr. The table has no singular overarching title visible at the top of the page itself, but its three column headers are **"Role," "Tech skills needed,"** and **"Why tech skills help."** There are no numerical data points, percentages, bar charts, axes, or quantitative figures anywhere in this table — it is entirely qualitative and descriptive in nature. The table contains six rows covering six distinct professional roles. The first role is **Technical Writer**, whose required tech skills include understanding of coding concepts, data analysis, and technical documentation tools, with specific examples listed as API, workflows UX, CMS, and AI tools; the rationale given is that technical writers need to explain complex technical information and that knowledge of coding and data analysis helps them understand and communicate technical content more effectively. The second role is **Product Manager**, requiring familiarity with software engineering processes, data analysis, and technical product features, with examples including data literacy, agile tools, APIs, and AI integration; the benefit stated is that tech skills enable collaboration with engineering teams, data-driven decision-making, and ensuring products meet technical requirements. The third role is **UX Designer**, with tech skills described partially in French — "Maîtrise des outils de design, des approches de recherche utilisateur et de la data analyse" — with examples including Figma, accessibility standards, CMS, and AI-assisted content; the rationale is that tech skills help in conducting user research, analyzing user data, and using design tools to create effective user experiences. The fourth role is **Community Manager**, requiring social media analytics, digital marketing tools, and data analysis, with examples including analytical dashboards, social media automation, and CRM; the benefit is measuring engagement, analyzing community data, and improving community strategies. The fifth role is **Business Development Executive**, requiring CRM software proficiency, data analysis, and digital marketing; tech skills help in managing client relationships using CRM tools, analyzing market data, and implementing digital marketing strategies. The sixth and final role is **Investment Banker**, requiring financial modeling software, data analysis, and risk management tools; the explanation notes that AI and machine learning can help derive and predict trading patterns, while NLP can read and analyze lengthy reports. The key insight of this table is that **tech skills are increasingly essential across a wide range of traditionally non-technical roles**, enabling professionals to make data-driven decisions, leverage automation, and collaborate more effectively with technical teams. The source is credited at the bottom of the page as **"Le Wagon © – All Rights Reserved,"** co-branded with **rhum:hr**, and this is page **6** of the document.

This is an infographic/slide (page 7 of a document) titled **"Increasing demand for tech skills in non tech roles"**. The visual combines a word cloud, bar chart-style data visualization, a pull quote, and descriptive text. The word cloud in the upper purple section displays various tech skills in varying font sizes indicating relative importance, including: Machine learning (largest), SQL, Python, AWS (Amazon Web Services), Azure, AI tools, Data visualization, Data Warehousing, ETL (Extract, Transform, Load), Predictive analysis, UX/UI Design, Software development, SEO (Search Engine Optimization), C++, Data Analysis, and C++. Below the word cloud, under the subheading **"Tech Skills, Essential by 2030"**, the document cites data from the **World Economic Forum (2025)** confirming that by 2030, technology skills will become essential across many industries. Two category groupings are presented: **AI & Big Data** and **Technological literacy**. Under AI & Big Data, three sectors are listed with exact percentages: Automotive and aerospace at **100%**, Telecommunications at **100%**, and Professional services at **98%**. Under Technological literacy, three sectors are listed: Automotive and aerospace at **84%**, Financial services at **84%**, and Healthcare services at **81%**. There are no traditional axis labels as these are horizontal pill-shaped bar indicators. A pull quote from **Pierre-Luc Labbée**, Founder and CEO of **rhum.hr**, states: *"When defining recruitment needs across non-tech sectors, we observe strong growth in the demand for technology and AI skills — particularly for the management and optimization of human and material resources, the automation of operations, and the use of tools for project management and internal and external communication."* The key insight is that tech skills — especially AI, Big Data, and technological literacy — are becoming essential in non-tech industries, with some sectors like Automotive/Aerospace and Telecommunications projected to require AI/Big Data skills at 100% by 2030, according to WEF 2025 data. The source is the **World Economic Forum (2025)**, and the document is published by **Le Wagon**, with collaboration from **rhum.hr**.

This is an infographic/editorial page from a PDF document. The page contains two main sections with text-based information panels rather than charts or graphs. The first heading reads "The most valued technical skills by companies in Canada include:" and covers four skill categories. The second heading reads "The most valued transversal skills by companies include:" with three purple pill-shaped buttons listing: "Problem-solving ability and critical thinking," "Adaptability, flexibility, and resilience," and "Communication." There are no axis labels or column headers as this is not a chart-based visual. The specific numerical data points mentioned are: up to **92%** of Canadian companies use cloud computing; generative AI could transform the daily activities of about **40% of the workforce**; and **SQL leads with 80% of job postings**, while Python and R stand out for advanced analytics. The key insights are that cloud computing expertise is nearly universal among Canadian companies (92%), AI will significantly impact 40% of workers, SQL dominates data job postings at 80%, and soft skills like problem-solving, adaptability, and communication are equally valued alongside technical skills. There is a photo of an audience attending what appears to be a tech event in the middle of the page. The source is identified at the bottom as **Le Wagon © – All Rights Reserved**, in partnership with **rhum hr**, and this is page **8** of the document.

This is an infographic/slide layout from a report. The heading is **"Most in-demand technical skills."** There are no numerical data points, percentages, bar charts, axes, or quantitative figures anywhere on this page — it is entirely text-based and categorical in nature. The page number visible is **9**, and the copyright line reads "Le Wagon © - All Rights Reserved." The infographic presents **13 skill category cards** arranged in a grid layout, each containing a bold category title and associated sub-skills: **Data Analytics** (SQL, Machine Learning, Data visualization); **AI** (Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing/NLP); **Cloud Management** (Architecture Cloud Management); **Cloud Computing** (Containerization tools/Docker, Orchestration tools/Kubernetes); **Cybersecurity** (Incident Management, Security Architecture, Cloud security); **AI** (Prompt engineering, Python); **Industrial Automation** (Machine learning, Data processing); **Programming** (Python, HTML, CSS, JavaScript); **Cybersecurity** (Risk management, Cryptography); **Data Management** (Python, SQL); **E-commerce** (SEO, Web analytics); **Software Development** (Python, JavaScript, Java); **Systems Maintenance** (Linux operations, Network Configuration and Troubleshooting); and **Advanced Data Analysis Skills** (SQL, Python, Data visualization/Tableau, Power BI). Below the cards are two expert quotes: **Remi Dion**, Co-founder and VP Applied AI at explor.ai, states that over the next five to ten years new foundational skills will emerge in AI governance, ethics, and system security; **Ivana Markovic**, Talent, Culture & Innovation at Osedea, emphasizes adaptability, communication, collaboration, and empathy as critical skills. The source is a co-publication by **Le Wagon** and **rhum hr**.

This is an infographic/slide page from a Le Wagon document. The page contains two distinct sections: a "Key skills in 2025" box in the upper right (paired with a photograph of three people collaborating over a laptop), and a "Most in-demand soft skills" grid at the bottom, with a "Build transferable skills" editorial section in between. There are no bar charts, scatter plots, or axes present — this is purely a text-and-layout infographic. The upper box is titled "Key skills in 2025" and lists eight checkmarked items: Analytical thinking, Resilience, flexibility and agility, Leadership and social influence, Creativity, Motivation and self-awareness, Technological literacy, Empathy and active listening, and Curiosity and lifelong learning, sourced from the World Economic Forum, 2025. The only explicit numeric reference is the year "2025" appearing both in the heading and the source citation. The bottom section is titled "Most in-demand soft skills" and displays twelve skills arranged in a three-row grid: Row 1 contains Critical thinking, Adaptability, Communication, and Problem solving; Row 2 contains Agility, Interpersonal skills, Resilience, and Organizational skills; Row 3 contains Team work, Leadership, Writing, Attention to detail, and Flexibility (five items in the third row). The editorial text states that the most sought-after profiles combine technical and soft skills, that flexibility and continuous learning are major assets in the Canadian job market, and that employers are looking for "a strong complementarity between the two." The page is numbered 10, and the document is credited to Le Wagon © – All Rights Reserved, co-branded with "rhum hr." No numerical data points, percentages, or statistics beyond the year references appear anywhere on the page.

This visual is an **infographic/content slide** from a PDF document. The main heading reads **"AI is not a threat. It's an opportunity."** The document references **PwC's 2025 AI Jobs Barometer**, described as "one of the most comprehensive studies to date on how artificial intelligence is impacting the world of work," which analyzed **nearly one billion job ads across six continents**. The specific data points and percentages visible are as follows: AI-exposed roles are seeing wage growth **up to 25% faster** than less exposed roles; roles requiring AI capabilities (such as prompt engineering, machine learning, or working with AI-powered tools) grew by **7.5% in the past year**; and **100% of industries studied** are increasing their use of AI. There are no axis labels or column headers, as this is a text-based infographic rather than a chart or table. The slide is divided into four sections: "AI-exposed roles are seeing faster wage growth," "Demand for AI-related skills keeps rising," "Productivity gains are real, and linked to human learning," and "The global shift is already happening." A closing quote is attributed to **Carol Stubbings, Global Chief Commercial Officer, PwC UK**, stating that the core challenge is not job scarcity but worker preparedness. The source is **PwC's 2025 AI Jobs Barometer**, and the document is branded by **Le Wagon** and **rhum hr**, with page number **11** visible at the bottom.

This visual is an infographic/editorial page from a PDF document. The title/heading is **"Canada, a hub for artificial intelligence."** The introductory text states that artificial intelligence and machine learning are at the forefront of Canada's technology sector, with strong research institutions and a focus on talent development. Within a purple highlighted box titled **"The Canadian AI hubs,"** the following specific data points appear: **Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal** are identified as the leading AI-development markets in Canada, accounting for **60% of the country's AI-specialty tech jobs**. It is further noted that the tech industry employs **almost half** of all AI-specialty talent, followed by the professional & business services and financial activities sectors, with the source cited as **CBRE**. There are no axis labels, column headers, bar charts, or tables present — this is a text-and-quote-based infographic layout. Three executive quotes are featured: **Christopher Moreno, CFO of MarineLabs**, states no one has been replaced and doesn't expect replacement soon, referencing the balance between science and art in programming. **Remi Dion, Co-founder and VP Applied AI at explor.ai**, describes AI as redefining priorities, methods, and client value through planning, forecasting, decision-making, and conversational tools. **Ivana Markovic, Talent, Culture & Innovation at Osedea**, notes AI expands the scope of problems solvable by combining software, robotics, and data. The page is attributed to **Le Wagon © – All Rights Reserved**, page **12**, and co-branded with **rhum hr**.

This is an infographic/slide combining a horizontal bar chart with a pull quote and contextual statistics. The title is "Growing skills needs across the Canadian job market" with the subtitle "Main technology skills shortages." The introductory text states that **43% of technology leaders report a skills gap within their department**, and **50%** of them say its impact has increased over the past year. The horizontal bar chart displays six technology skill shortage categories with their corresponding percentages, listed from highest to lowest as follows: AI, machine learning, and data science at **56%**; IT operations and support at **39%**; Cybersecurity and data protection at **36%**; ERP/CRM development and management at **27%**; Cloud architecture and operations at **22%**; and Networking, cloud, and systems at **18%**. There are no axis labels explicitly labeled on the chart — the bars are labeled directly with their percentage values inside or beside the bars. The bars are color-coded from dark purple (highest) to light purple/lavender (lowest). Below the chart, a pull quote from **Pete Brown, Global Workforce Leader, PwC UK**, states that core skills used to last **4 to 6 years**, but now in an AI era, skills are rapidly changing every **18 months** or **12 months**. The key insight is that AI/ML/data science represents the most critical skills gap in Canadian tech departments, and workforce skills are becoming obsolete at an accelerating pace. The source cited is **Robert Half, 2025**, and the document is credited to **Le Wagon**, with a co-branding mark for **rhum hr**, on page **13**.

This visual is an infographic/document page combining text, highlighted statistics, and bullet points in a structured layout. The title or heading is **"The need for hands-on, lifelong learning."** The numbers and data points present are as follows: **66%** — the skills sought by employers are changing 66% faster in jobs most vs least exposed to AI, described as more than 2.5x faster than last year, sourced from PwC; **3x** — students who applied skills in practice with immediate feedback learned three times more efficiently than those who learned by lecture alone, sourced from Carnegie Mellon; **×8** — increase in the likelihood of being considered for a position in Canada, with ×12 specifically for AI-related roles; **50%** — share of core skills required to qualify instead of an exact match to title or experience; **+24%** — growth in female representation within AI talent pools; **+6%** — additional increase in opportunities for workers without a university degree compared to degree holders; **2.5x** faster than last year (referenced in the 66% stat); and **half** of required skills being sufficient to attract recruiter attention. There are no axis labels or column headers, as this is not a chart. The key insight is that hands-on, skills-based learning and hiring are replacing degree-based models, dramatically expanding workforce inclusion and opportunity — particularly for those without traditional credentials. The sources cited include **PwC**, **Carnegie Mellon**, **Robert Half 2024**, **McKinsey and TechnoCompétences 2024**, and the **LinkedIn Economic Graph Research Institute**.

This is an infographic/report page (page 15) from a Le Wagon document. The page does not contain any charts, graphs, tables, or data visualizations with numerical data points, percentages, or axes. Instead, it contains a pull quote from **Ivana Markovic**, Talent, Culture & Innovation at Osedea, which reads: "Cross-disciplinary skills will become more valuable. We're preparing by creating an environment where people are encouraged to learn constantly, experiment, and stay curious. Our philosophy is that growth is a constant: if you stop learning, you fall behind." Below this is a purple conclusion box stating that candidates should focus on developing and showcasing skills rather than relying on job titles or traditional degrees, emphasizing that employers seek both technical and human/interpersonal skills, and that individuals should "train themselves, stay informed, and use AI as a driver of performance, optimization, and development." The lower section is titled **"Explore Le Wagon alumni success stories"** and features four alumni profiles: **Sofia A.** (From Pastry Chef to Backend Developer), **Paul J.** (From a PhD in philosophy to Data Scientist), **Morgane S.** (From Supply Chain Analyst to Manager, BI & Analytics), and **Thomas B.** (From Marketing Consultant to AI Engineer). There are no numerical data points, percentages, or axis labels anywhere on this page. The source/footer reads "Le Wagon © - All Rights Reserved" with co-branding from **Le Wagon** and **rhum hr**, and the page number is **15**.

This visual is an informational slide or infographic page from a PDF document. The heading reads **"Une initiative Le Wagon & rhum.hr"** (A Le Wagon & rhum.hr initiative). There are no charts, graphs, axes, or column headers present — instead, the page contains two company profile sections with descriptive text, logos, photographs, and call-to-action buttons. The specific numbers and data points visible are as follows: Le Wagon was **founded in Paris in 2013**, operates in **+40 cities**, across **25 countries, including Montreal (Quebec, Canada)**, and has a community of **31,000+ graduates**. Rhum.hr was **founded in Montreal in 2017** and now has offices in **Vancouver and Barcelona**. The page number shown at the bottom is **16**. The two call-to-action buttons read **"Discover our courses"** (in purple, associated with Le Wagon) and **"Learn more"** (in purple, associated with rhum.hr). The footer reads **"Le Wagon © - All Rights Reserved"**. The key takeaway is that this slide introduces a joint initiative between Le Wagon, a global immersive tech training organization, and rhum.hr, an international HR and talent acquisition agency, combining tech education with human resources expertise. The source credited is **Le Wagon ©**, as indicated in the footer.

This is a slide (presentation page) from a document produced by Le Wagon. The title/heading is **"Merci à nos partenaires"** (Thank you to our partners), with two subsections labeled **"Partenaires collaborateurs"** (Collaborative partners) and **"Partenaires de diffusion"** (Distribution/Broadcasting partners). There are no numerical data points, percentages, bar charts, axes, or quantitative information present on this slide. The only number visible is the page number **17** in the bottom right corner. The slide is purely a partner acknowledgment page displaying logos. Under "Partenaires collaborateurs," three logos are shown: **/OSEDEA**, **explor.ai**, and **MarineLabs Data Systems**. Under "Partenaires de diffusion," nine partner logos are displayed: **Techno Compétences**, **Desjardins Caisse des Technologies de l'information**, **Réseau Action TI**, **AQi (Le réseau des consultants indépendants en TI, 30 ans déjà)**, **Tail'ed**, **Kumojin**, **Queertech**, **Women Techmakers Montreal**, **Women in Tech Canada**, and one additional logo that is partially legible. The source is identified at the bottom as **Le Wagon © – Tous droits réservés**, with the Le Wagon and Rhum HR logos also present in the footer. The key takeaway is a formal acknowledgment of the event's collaborative and distribution partners.

This is a bibliography/reference page (slide) from a document produced by Le Wagon, page 17 of the document. The heading is simply "Bibliography" in bold. There are no charts, graphs, axes, percentages, or numerical data points present on this page — it is purely a formatted list of citations and references. The sources cited include: Robert Half (2025) "Building Future Forward Tech teams. Technology skills and solutions to drive business and IT transformation"; Made in CA (January 16, 2025) "Cloud Computing Statistics in Canada"; Randstad "Your ultimate guide to trending job skills in 2025"; Information and Communications Technology Council (ICTC) (August 2025) "Digital Economy Pulse: Productivity and Employment Trends in Canada"; Western Community College (October 2025) "Future of Tech Careers in Canada"; PwC CA "Generative AI and Canadian businesses"; Robert Half "Canada Technology Salaries and Trends. 2026 Canada Salary Guide"; Robert Half (June 18, 2025) "2025 Canada Job Market: Tech Hiring Trends and In-Demand Roles"; Technocompétences (April 2025); Banque de développement du Canada BDC (December 16, 2024); Polytechnics Canada (April 2025); Carnegie Mellon University (May 30, 2025); Canadian Federation of Independent Business (2025 Q1); CompTIA (2024); LinkedIn Economic Graph Research Institute (March 3, 2025); CBRE 2024 and CBRE 2025 "Scoring Tech Talent"; Robert Half (December 19, 2024); PwC (2025) "The Fearless Future: 2025 Global AI Jobs Barometer"; World Economic Forum (January 7, 2025); Axcess Talent Management Solutions Inc (September 23, 2025); ICTC "Onwards and Upwards. Digital Talent Outlook 2025"; Nucamp (2025); Robert Half (April 21, 2025); and The Career Accelerator (April 3, 2025). The key takeaway is that this page documents all research sources used throughout the report, drawing from a wide range of Canadian and global organizations. The footer reads "Le Wagon © - All Rights Reserved" with co-branding from Le Wagon and rhum hr.
